Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) integrate computational and physical components with distributed sensing and control.
Data injection attacks (DIAs) compromise measurement integrity to disrupt state estimation without triggering bad data detection.
The paper models decentralized DIAs where multiple attackers independently inject random Gaussian attack vectors.
State variables are modeled as zero-mean multivariate Gaussian with known covariance matrix.
Measurements follow a linearized model corrupted by additive white Gaussian noise.
The attack vector is modeled as a zero-mean multivariate Gaussian with covariance matrix representing attack power.
Disruption is quantified by the mutual information I(X;Y_A) between state variables and compromised measurements.
Stealthiness is quantified by the Kullback-Leibler divergence D(P_{Y_A} || P_Y) between attacked and normal measurement distributions.
The decentralized attack problem is formulated as a potential game with convex potential functions.
The Nash equilibrium of the game is proven to exist and be unique under the proposed formulation.
Attackers do not require coordination due to the independence assumption of attack vectors.
A best response dynamics algorithm is proposed to reach the Nash equilibrium in decentralized settings.
Numerical results on IEEE test systems validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate attack feasibility.
Global detection uses joint measurement distributions, while local detection uses individual measurement statistics.
The Gaussian assumption maximizes entropy for fixed covariance, minimizing inductive bias in modeling.
The attack cost function balances maximizing disruption and minimizing detection probability.
The covariance matrix of the compromised measurements includes contributions from system noise and attack covariance.
Decentralized stealth attacks pose a practical threat due to minimal coordination requirements among attackers.
Information-theoretic measures provide a fundamental limit perspective on attack impact and detectability.
The paper contributes a novel framework combining Bayesian estimation, information theory, and game theory for CPS security.
